vsm1.3:112.1: If that is so, then is what is called “the measurelessness of the object of jhāna produced on foulness” contradicted?
vsm1.3:112.3: For one man apprehends the sign in a large bloated corpse or skeleton, another in a small one.
vsm1.3:112.4: In this way the jhāna of the one has a limited object and of the other a measureless object.
vsm1.3:112.5:
Or alternatively, “With a measureless object” (Dhs 182–84 in elision) is said of it
referring to one who extends it, seeing no disadvantage in doing so.
vsm1.3:112.6: But it need not be extended because no benefit results.
vsm1.3:113.1: The rest need not be extended likewise.
vsm1.3:113.3: When a man extends the sign of in-breaths and out-breaths,
vsm1.3:113.4: only a quantity of wind is extended,
vsm1.3:113.5: and it has a definite location, the nose-tip.
vsm1.3:113.6: So it need not be extended because of the disadvantage and because of the definiteness of the location.
vsm1.3:113.7: And the divine abidings have living beings as their object.
vsm1.3:113.8: When a man extends the sign of these, only the quantity of living beings would be extended,
vsm1.3:113.9: and there is no purpose in that.
vsm1.3:113.10: So that also need not be extended.
vsm1.3:114.1: When it is said, “Intent upon one quarter with his heart endued with loving-kindness” (D I 250), etc.,
vsm1.3:114.2: that is said for the sake of comprehensive inclusion.
vsm1.3:114.3: For it is when a man develops it progressively by including living beings in one direction by one house, by two houses, etc.,
vsm1.3:114.4: that he is said to be “intent upon one direction,”
vsm1.3:114.5: not when he extends the sign.
vsm1.3:114.6: And there is no counterpart sign here that he might extend.
vsm1.3:114.7: Also the state of having a limited or measureless object can be understood here according to the way of inclusion, too.
vsm1.3:115.1: As regards the immaterial states as object, space need not be extended since it is the mere removal of the kasiṇa materiality;
vsm1.3:115.2: for that should be brought to mind only as the disappearance of the kasiṇa materiality;
vsm1.3:115.3: if he extends it, nothing further happens.
vsm1.3:115.4: And consciousness need not be extended since it is a state consisting in an individual essence,
vsm1.3:115.5: and it is not possible to extend a state consisting in an individual essence.
vsm1.3:115.6: The disappearance of consciousness need not be extended since it is mere non-existence of consciousness.
vsm1.3:115.7: And the base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception as object
vsm1.3:115.8: need not be extended since it too is a state consisting in an individual essence.
vsm1.3:116.1: The rest need not be extended because they have no sign.
vsm1.3:116.2: For it is the counterpart sign that would be extendable,
vsm1.3:116.3: and the object of the recollection of the Buddha, etc., is not a counterpart sign.
vsm1.3:116.4: Consequently there is no need for extension there.
vsm1.3:116.5: This is “as to extension and non-extension.”
vsm1.3:117.3:
twenty-two have counterpart signs as object, that is to say, the ten kasiṇas, the ten kinds of foulness,
mindfulness of breathing, and mindfulness occupied with the body;
vsm1.3:117.4: the rest do not have counterpart signs as object.
vsm1.3:117.5:
Then twelve have states consisting in individual essences as object, that is to say, eight of the ten
recollections—except mindfulness of breathing and mindfulness occupied with the body—
vsm1.3:117.6: the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment,
vsm1.3:117.8: the base consisting of boundless consciousness,
vsm1.3:117.9: and the base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception;
vsm1.3:117.10: and twenty-two have counterpart signs as object, that is to say, the ten kasiṇas, the ten kinds of foulness,
vsm1.3:117.11: mindfulness of breathing, and mindfulness occupied with the body;
vsm1.3:117.12: while the remaining six have “not-so-classifiable” objects.
vsm1.3:117.13:
Then eight have mobile objects in the early stage though the counterpart is stationary,
that is to say, the festering, the bleeding, the worm-infested,
vsm1.3:117.15: the water kasiṇa, the fire kasiṇa, the air kasiṇa,
vsm1.3:117.16: and in the case of the light kasiṇa the object consisting of a circle of sunlight, etc.;
vsm1.3:117.17: the rest have immobile objects. This is “as to object.”
vsm1.3:118.2:
here the twelve, namely, the ten kinds of foulness, mindfulness
occupied with the body, and perception of repulsiveness in nutriment,
vsm1.3:118.4: These twelve and mindfulness of breathing do not occur in the Brahmā-world.
vsm1.3:118.5: But none except the four immaterial states occur in the immaterial becoming.
vsm1.3:118.6: All occur among human beings. This is “as to plane.”
vsm1.3:119.1: 8. As to apprehending: here the exposition should be understood according to the seen, the touched and the heard.
vsm1.3:119.2: Herein, these nineteen, that is to say, nine kasiṇas omitting the air kasiṇa and the ten kinds of foulness,
vsm1.3:119.3: must be apprehended by the seen.
vsm1.3:119.4: The meaning is that in the early stage their sign must be apprehended by constantly looking with the eye.
vsm1.3:119.5: In the case of mindfulness occupied with the body the five parts ending with skin must be apprehended by the seen
vsm1.3:119.6: and the rest by the heard,
vsm1.3:119.7: so its object must be apprehended by the seen and the heard.
vsm1.3:119.8: Mindfulness of breathing must be apprehended by the touched;
vsm1.3:119.9: the air kasiṇa by the seen and the touched;
vsm1.3:119.10: the remaining eighteen by the heard.
vsm1.3:119.11: The divine abiding of equanimity and the four immaterial states are not apprehendable by a beginner;
vsm1.3:119.12: but the remaining thirty-five are. This is “as to apprehending.”
vsm1.3:120.1: 9. As to condition: of these meditation subjects nine kasiṇas omitting the space kasiṇa are conditions for the immaterial states.
vsm1.3:120.2: The ten kasiṇas are conditions for the kinds of direct-knowledge.
vsm1.3:120.3: Three divine abidings are conditions for the fourth divine abiding.
vsm1.3:120.4: Each lower immaterial state is a condition for each higher one.
vsm1.3:120.5: The base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception is a condition for the attainment of cessation.
vsm1.3:120.6: All are conditions for living in bliss, for insight, and for the fortunate kinds of becoming. This is “as to condition.”
vsm1.3:121.1: 10. As to suitability to temperament: here the exposition should be understood according to what is suitable to the temperaments.
vsm1.3:121.3:
first, the ten kinds of foulness and mindfulness occupied with the body are eleven
meditation subjects suitable for one of greedy temperament.
vsm1.3:121.4: The four divine abidings and four colour kasiṇas are eight suitable for one of hating temperament.
vsm1.3:121.5:
Mindfulness of breathing is the one recollection as a meditation subject suitable for one of deluded
temperament and for one of speculative temperament.
vsm1.3:121.6: The first six recollections are suitable for one of faithful temperament.
vsm1.3:121.7: Mindfulness of death, the recollection of peace,
vsm1.3:121.8:
the defining of the four elements, and the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment,
are four suitable for one of intelligent temperament.
vsm1.3:121.9: The remaining kasiṇas and the immaterial states are suitable for all kinds of temperament.
vsm1.3:121.10: And anyone of the kasiṇas should be limited for one of speculative temperament and measureless for one of deluded temperament.
vsm1.3:121.11: This is how the exposition should be understood here “as to suitability to temperament.”
vsm1.3:122.1: All this has been stated in the form of direct opposition and complete suitability.
vsm1.3:122.2: But there is actually no profitable development that does not suppress greed, etc., and help faith, and so on.
vsm1.3:122.3: And this is said in the Meghiya Sutta:
vsm1.3:122.4: “One should, in addition, develop these four things:
vsm1.3:122.5: foulness should be developed for the purpose of abandoning greed (lust).
vsm1.3:122.6: Loving-kindness should be developed for the purpose of abandoning ill will.
vsm1.3:122.7: Mindfulness of breathing should be developed for the purpose of cutting off applied thought.
vsm1.3:122.8: Perception of impermanence should be cultivated for the purpose of eliminating the conceit, ‘I am’” (A IV 358).
vsm1.3:122.9: Also in the Rāhula Sutta, in the passage beginning, “Develop loving-kindness, Rāhula” (M I 424),
vsm1.3:122.10: seven meditation subjects are given for a single temperament.
vsm1.3:122.11: So instead of insisting on the mere letter, the intention should be sought in each instance.
vsm1.3:122.12:
This is the explanatory exposition of the meditation subject referred to by the words
he should apprehend…one meditation subject (§28).
vsm1.3:123.1: Now the words and he should apprehend are illustrated as follows.
vsm1.3:123.2:
After approaching the good friend of the kind described in the explanation of the words then
approach the good friend, the giver of a meditation subject (§28 and §57–73),
vsm1.3:123.3: the meditator should dedicate himself to the Blessed One, the Enlightened One, or to a teacher,
vsm1.3:123.4: and he should ask for the meditation subject with a sincere inclination of the heart and sincere resolution.
vsm1.3:124.1:
Herein, he should dedicate himself to the Blessed One, the Enlightened One, in this way:
“Blessed One, I relinquish this my person to you.”
vsm1.3:124.2: For without having thus dedicated himself, when living in a remote abode
vsm1.3:124.3: he might be unable to stand fast if a frightening object made its appearance,
vsm1.3:124.4: and he might return to a village abode,
vsm1.3:124.8: But when he has dedicated himself in this way no fear arises in him if a frightening object makes its appearance;
vsm1.3:124.9: in fact only joy arises in him as he reflects: “Have you not wisely already dedicated yourself to the Enlightened One?”
vsm1.3:125.1: Suppose a man had a fine piece of Kāsi cloth. He would feel grief if it were eaten by rats or moths;
vsm1.3:125.2: but if he gave it to a bhikkhu needing robes,
vsm1.3:125.3: he would feel only joy if he saw the bhikkhu tearing it up to make his patched cloak.
vsm1.3:125.4: And so it is with this.
vsm1.3:126.1: When he dedicates himself to a teacher, he should say: “I relinquish this my person to you, venerable sir.”
vsm1.3:126.2: For one who has not dedicated his person thus becomes unresponsive to correction,
vsm1.3:126.3: hard to speak to, and unamenable to advice,
vsm1.3:126.4: or he goes where he likes without asking the teacher.
vsm1.3:126.5: Consequently the teacher does not help him with either material things or the Dhamma,
vsm1.3:126.6: and he does not train him in the cryptic books.
vsm1.3:126.7: Failing to get these two kinds of help,
vsm1.3:126.8: he finds no footing in the Dispensation,
vsm1.3:126.9: and he soon comes down to misconducting himself or to the lay state.
vsm1.3:126.10: But if he has dedicated his person, he is not unresponsive to correction,
vsm1.3:126.11: does not go about as he likes,
vsm1.3:126.12: is easy to speak to, and lives only in dependence on the teacher.
vsm1.3:126.13: He gets the twofold help from the teacher
vsm1.3:126.14: and attains growth, increase, and fulfilment in the Dispensation.
vsm1.3:127.1: Three bhikkhus came to the elder, it seems.
vsm1.3:127.3: “Venerable sir, I am ready to fall from a cliff the height of one hundred men, if it is said to be to your advantage.”
vsm1.3:127.5:
“Venerable sir, I am ready to grind away this body from the heels up without
remainder on a flat stone, if it is said to be to your advantage.”
vsm1.3:127.6: The third said, “Venerable sir, I am ready to die by stopping breathing, if it is said to be to your advantage.”
vsm1.3:127.7: Observing, “These bhikkhus are certainly capable of progress,” the elder expounded a meditation subject to them.
vsm1.3:127.8: Following his advice, the three attained Arahantship. This is the benefit in self-dedication.
vsm1.3:127.9: Hence it was said above “dedicating himself to the Blessed One, the Enlightened One, or to a teacher.”
vsm1.3:128.1: With a sincere inclination of the heart and sincere resolution (§123):
vsm1.3:128.2: the meditator’s inclination should be sincere in the six modes beginning with non-greed.
vsm1.3:128.3: For it is one of such sincere inclination who arrives at one of the three kinds of enlightenment,
vsm1.3:128.5: “Six kinds of inclination lead to the maturing of the enlightenment of the Bodhisattas.
vsm1.3:128.6: With the inclination to non-greed, Bodhisattas see the fault in greed.
vsm1.3:128.7: With the inclination to non-hate, Bodhisattas see the fault in hate.
vsm1.3:128.8: With the inclination to non-delusion, Bodhisattas see the fault in delusion.
vsm1.3:128.9: With the inclination to renunciation, Bodhisattas see the fault in house life.
vsm1.3:128.10: With the inclination to seclusion, Bodhisattas see the fault in society.
vsm1.3:128.11: With the inclination to relinquishment, Bodhisattas see the fault in all kinds of becoming and destiny (Source untraced.)”
vsm1.3:128.12:
For stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, those with cankers destroyed (i.e. Arahants),
Paccekabuddhas, and Fully Enlightened Ones, whether past, future or present,
vsm1.3:128.13: all arrive at the distinction peculiar to each by means of these same six modes.
vsm1.3:128.14: That is why he should have sincerity of inclination in these six modes.
vsm1.3:129.1: He should be whole-heartedly resolved on that.
vsm1.3:129.2: The meaning is that he should be resolved upon concentration, respect concentration, incline to concentration,
vsm1.3:129.3: be resolved upon Nibbāna, respect Nibbāna, incline to Nibbāna.
vsm1.3:130.1: When, with sincerity of inclination and whole-hearted resolution in this way, he asks for a meditation subject,
vsm1.3:130.2: then a teacher who has acquired the penetration of minds can know his temperament by surveying his mental conduct;
vsm1.3:130.3: and a teacher who has not can know it by putting such questions to him as:
vsm1.3:130.5: or “What states are usually present in you?”
vsm1.3:130.6: or “What do you like bringing to mind?”
vsm1.3:130.7: or “What meditation subject does your mind favour?”
vsm1.3:130.8: When he knows, he can expound a meditation subject suitable to that temperament.
vsm1.3:130.9: And in doing so, he can expound it in three ways:
vsm1.3:130.10: it can be expounded to one who has already learnt the meditation subject by having him recite it at one or two sessions;
vsm1.3:130.11: it can be expounded to one who lives in the same place each time he comes;
vsm1.3:130.12: and to one who wants to learn it and then go elsewhere
vsm1.3:130.13: it can be expounded in such a manner that it is neither too brief nor too long.
vsm1.3:131.1: Herein, when first he is explaining the earth kasiṇa, there are nine aspects that he should explain. They are
vsm1.3:131.2: the four faults of the kasiṇa,
vsm1.3:131.4: the method of development for one who has made it,
vsm1.3:131.7: the seven kinds of suitable and unsuitable,
vsm1.3:131.8: the ten kinds of skill in absorption,
vsm1.3:131.11: In the case of the other meditation subjects, each should be expounded in the way appropriate to it.
vsm1.3:131.12: All this will be made clear in the directions for development.
vsm1.3:131.13: But when the meditation subject is being expounded in this way, the meditator must apprehend the sign as he listens.
vsm1.3:132.1: Apprehend the sign means that he must connect each aspect thus:
vsm1.3:132.7: When he listens attentively, apprehending the sign in this way, his meditation subject is well apprehended.
vsm1.3:132.8: Then, and because of that, he successfully attains distinction, but not otherwise.
vsm1.3:132.9: This clarifies the meaning of the words “and he must apprehend.”
vsm1.3:133.2: approach the good friend, the giver of a meditation subject,
vsm1.3:133.3: and he should apprehend from among the forty meditation subjects one that suits his own temperament (§28)
vsm1.3:133.4: have been expounded in detail in all their aspects.
vsm1.3:133.5:
The third chapter called “The Description of Taking a Meditation Subject” in the Treatise on the Development
of Concentration in the Path of Purification composed for the purpose of gladdening good people.
